outcome: The conjecture itself (infinitely many primes of the form n^2+1) remains completely open since 26 January 2024; only proxy quantities in the surrounding literature (the exponent c such that the largest prime factor of n^2+1 infinitely often exceeds n^c, and the Mahler-Chowla-type lower bound on the log-growth of that largest prime factor) have moved, and per the infinitude-only-moves-when-answered rule none of these settle or restrict the stated question.
summary: The stated question — are there infinitely many primes of the form n^2+1 (Landau's fourth problem) — remains fully open, with no proof, disproof, or answered case since 26 January 2024. What has moved since the frozen revision is a cluster of closely related but distinct quantities in the surrounding research literature, none of which is the infinitude question itself and none of which restricts it in the §3.1 sense of settling a genuine case (they narrow where a large prime factor could be found, not whether infinitely many primes n^2+1 exist): (1) the exponent c for which the largest prime factor of n^2+1 infinitely often exceeds n^c — Merikoski's n^1.279 (Inventiones, published 2024 but first posted to arXiv in 2019, hence 'open_stale'-flavoured and pre-window in substance) was improved to n^1.3 by Alexandru Pascadi (arXiv:2404.04239, posted 5 Apr 2024, revised through Jan 2026), then to n^1.317 by Runbo Li (arXiv:2406.07575, posted 6 Jun 2024), and unconditionally to n^1.312 by Grimmelt & Merikoski (matching a value Merikoski had previously only obtained conditionally on the Selberg eigenvalue conjecture); and (2) the Mahler-Chowla-type absolute lower bound on the growth rate of the largest prime factor, improved by Hector Pasten from (log_2 n)^2/log_3 n (2023, pre-window) to (log_2 n)^2/log_4 n in arXiv:2609.01327, posted 1 Sept 2026. None of these move the needle on 'infinitely many primes of the form n^2+1' as such — even a hypothetical proof that the largest prime factor exceeds n^2 (Landau's original heuristic target) would not by itself prove infinitude, since a large prime factor is not the value n^2+1 itself being prime. I read this as squarely in §3.1's 'related problem/quantity' category rather than a 'case' of the stated bullet, so status is open/no_change_found rather than progress, even though the triage flagged real movement in the adjacent literature. The single most interesting item found is arXiv:2609.01327 (Pasten, 1 Sept 2026): its acknowledgements state, verbatim, 'Corollary 1.2 and its initial proof were first obtained in an autonomous way by the AI model ChatGPT-5.6 Sol Pro after a single prompt in July 2026. Theorem 1.1 was subsequently discovered by the author from interactions with the same AI model. The proof presented here is due to the author. Claude Opus 5 was used for proofreading an earlier version of the manuscript.' This is confirmed on both the arXiv HTML rendering and the independent Pith Review summary of the same paper, so it is not a fetch artifact. However this AI involvement (a) concerns the Mahler-Chowla log-growth bound, a quantity even further removed from the stated infinitude question than the n^1.3-type exponent chain, and (b) the paper is a preprint with no expert digestion yet found. Because the underlying mathematical event is not in scope for this bullet under §3.1, I am not coding this record as ai_role other than none — the AI involvement is real but attaches to a related-problem result, not to this problem. I record its existence here for transparency but do not let it drive the classification of this record, consistent with the instruction not to let a dramatic-looking result pull a no-change record toward a false positive.
competing_reading: A case could be made that the largest-prime-factor exponent bound (n^1.3, n^1.312, n^1.317) is a genuine 'case' of Landau's fourth problem in the §3.1 sense, since it directly measures how close the literature has come to Landau's own heuristic (exponent 2 would essentially force infinitely many primes via a Chebyshev-type argument on the cofactor). Under that reading this record would be 'progress' with ai_role 'none' for the exponent chain (Pascadi/Li/Grimmelt-Merikoski papers show no AI involvement), and the Pasten log-growth paper (arXiv:2609.01327) would still be a separate, more tangential item. Even under this more generous reading, however, the AI-touched paper (2609.01327) is about the log-growth bound rather than the exponent-c bound, so it would still not be the item that drives an 'assisted' or 'generated' ai_role for this specific bullet — at most it would be noted as adjacent incident-like context. I am fairly confident 'open'/'no_change_found' is the correct call for the bullet as literally worded, but flag this as the strongest alternative.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) that n^2+1 is prime for infinitely many n, or an expert ruling that one of the largest-prime-factor bounds (e.g. reaching exponent 2, per Landau's own remark) is understood to formally imply the infinitude statement — no source found makes that implication explicit or claims it has been reached.
